//: cxagent configuration. Copy to ~/.config/cxagent/config.json and edit.
Every block is OPTIONAL except `providers` — without one there is no model to talk to,
and cxagent starts into its setup wizard instead.
AN UNKNOWN KEY IS IGNORED; AN UNKNOWN VALUE IS AN ERROR. There is no key-level
validation, so a misspelled key name is silent — `contextWindwo` simply does nothing.
Values are checked: an unknown provider `kind`, or a name referencing a provider that
is not configured, stops startup and says so. Check that a key took effect rather than
JSON has no comments. These `//` arrays are data the parser ignores, which is the
conventional way to annotate a JSON sample and the reason they read oddly.
//providers: THE MODEL CATALOG. Each entry is an INSTANCE: a name you choose, bound to one endpoint
and one model. Names are referenced elsewhere in this file — `defaultProvider` and, from
contextWindow: the model's REAL context size in tokens. It is the denominator for the
occupancy readout and the trigger for compaction.
OPTIONAL, AND CONFIGURED WINS OVER PROBED. Absent, cxagent asks the endpoint at startup
(bounded at three seconds; any failure just leaves it unknown, and an unknown window
means compaction falls back to a fixed threshold). Setting it explicitly is you saying
something the server cannot know — a shared endpoint, a deliberately smaller budget —
and a number read off the server must not override that.
Do not set it LARGER than the endpoint really allows. Nothing compacts until the
provider rejects the request, and that failure arrives mid-work with no warning.

//maxConcurrentAgents: How many sub-agents may call THIS endpoint at once. Absent or 0 = unlimited (the default).
cxagent cannot discover what an endpoint tolerates, so it does not guess — set this when
you know. A single-threaded local server queues concurrent children at the socket and
splits its context across slots; a hosted API answers them and returns 429s.
See CONFIG.md. The real bound on a run is orchestrator.maxTurns, not this.

//defaultProvider: Which instance an agent uses when nothing else says. A name from `providers`.
//classifier: Which instance reviews actions in `/mode edits auto`. A name from `providers`, or absent.
ABSENT MEANS AUTO IS NOT OFFERED — not listed by /mode, not reachable by Shift+Tab, not
parseable as a flag. A mode that claims background review while nothing reviews is worse
A REMOTE INSTANCE AVOIDS EVICTING THE SESSION. A local endpoint on --parallel 1 has one
slot: a classifier call parks the session's prefix to host RAM and restores it (measured
at 28ms for 20k tokens against 5,850ms cold), which is survivable but not free. A separate
Cost is small either way: measured against gemini-2.5-flash-lite, one classification is
Auto FAILS CLOSED. A timeout, a transport error, a malformed reply or an unrecognised
verdict all ask; only an explicit allow is silent.
//agents: SUB-AGENT TYPES (step 2). A name, a briefing, and optionally a provider.
description: WHEN to choose this type, for the PARENT deciding. One line. It is the only
thing the model sees before picking, so write the situation rather than the job:
"when finding something means reading across several files", not "searches files".
Optional. Without it the catalog falls back to the briefing's first sentence, which is
written for the CHILD and reads as an instruction — "You search and report" tells a
chooser nothing about when to reach for it.
briefing: HOW this agent works. It becomes the highest-authority text in the child's
system prompt — above the general prompt and above anything the parent tells it — so it
is the one instruction channel a human writes and a model cannot override.
provider: an instance name from `providers` above. Omit to use the parent's. A name that
is not in `providers` is a startup error, not a surprise at spawn time.
maxTurns: how many turns this type gets before it stops and summarises what it has. Omit
to inherit the session ceiling (`orchestrator.maxTurns`), which is the right
default and what every child got before this key existed.
SET IT ONLY WHEN THE JOB HAS A KNOWN SHAPE. A search that should take four turns and
takes forty is worth stopping; open-ended work is not. The failure mode is specific and
has bitten this project before: a cap that fires mid-work does not fail loudly, it
returns a SALVAGE SUMMARY of unfinished work, and a caller that cannot tell that from a
finished answer acts on it. cxagent marks it (state="capped" in the result) — but a
number set too low turns every run of that type into a half-answer.
0 means no cap, as it does for the session.
A BRIEFING IS A REQUEST, NOT A PERMISSION. 'Never edit files' asks the agent not to; it
does not remove the tool. Enforcement is a separate mechanism and does not exist yet, so
do not rely on a briefing to contain an agent.
`general` always exists whether or not it appears here — same model as the parent, no
briefing. Define it to give every untyped sub-agent a standing instruction.
A type does NOT get its own turn ceiling or token budget. Those are session-wide
(`orchestrator` below), and a child inherits them.

explore.description: when answering means reading across several files and you want the conclusion rather than the file dumps. Give it a question, not a location. It returns exact paths as file_path:line_number and says plainly when the thing does not exist — a confident negative is a real answer. It does not edit anything. USE THE PLANNER INSTEAD when what you want back is a design rather than a fact: a planner reads code too, so sending an explorer to plan something gets you a report about the code as it is, which is not a plan and cannot be built from. WHEN YOU PASS ITS FINDINGS ON, put them in `context`, not in the prompt — context stays with the next agent for its whole run, a prompt does not survive a long one, and an agent that loses the facts you gave it goes and reads the same files again.
explore.briefing: You search and report. Find what was asked for, give exact paths as file_path:line_number, and say what you actually saw rather than what you expect to be true. Do not edit anything. If the thing asked for does not appear to exist, say so and say where you looked — a confident negative is an answer, and is worth more than more searching. Before you report a path, check it against what you actually opened.

review.description: when you want code checked for correctness — logic that is wrong rather than style that is unusual. Best on a diff or a named set of files. It returns specific objections with a failing case behind each one, and says plainly when something is fine rather than inventing concerns.
review.briefing: You review code for correctness. Look for logic that is wrong rather than style that is unusual, and say plainly when something is fine. An objection with no failing case behind it is noise.

test.description: when tests need running and a failure needs diagnosing. It reads the actual output before drawing a conclusion — a command that exits 0 has not necessarily verified anything, and a filter that matched nothing exits 0 too — and reports the counts it saw rather than the counts it expected.
test.briefing: You run and diagnose tests. Read the actual output before drawing a conclusion — a command that exits 0 has not necessarily verified anything, and a filter that matched nothing exits 0. Report the counts you saw.

planner.description: when the change should be thought through before any of it is written, or when you are not sure the request is possible as asked. IT DOES ITS OWN READING — you do not need to explore first, and sending an explorer to design something gets you a description of the code rather than a plan for changing it. BUT IF YOU HAVE ALREADY EXPLORED, hand what was found to it in `context` rather than the prompt: otherwise it re-reads the whole codebase to rediscover what you already knew, and may spend its run doing that instead of writing the plan. It reads enough to be specific, writes the plan to a file under ./plans/, and ends its answer with PLAN WRITTEN: <path> so you can tell a plan from a report at a glance. Its answer covers what the change is, the steps in order, which step is most likely to be wrong, and anything it found that changes the shape of the work — including a reason it cannot be done as asked. It changes nothing else.
planner.briefing: Your one deliverable is a plan FILE. Before you finish you must call write_file to create ./plans/<short-name>.md containing the plan, and your answer must end with the line PLAN WRITTEN: ./plans/<short-name>.md — exactly that, on its own line, nothing after it. A run that investigates well and ends without that file has failed, however good the reading was: whoever asked has nothing to build from, and nothing to review. If you find yourself about to stop, check first that you have written it. READ ONLY UNTIL YOU CAN BE SPECIFIC, then stop and write. You do not need to understand the whole codebase; you need to name the files that must change and what each change is. When you can do that, you are done reading — further reading is not making the plan better, it is postponing it. In the file: what the change is and why it takes that shape, the steps in the order they can be made without breaking the build in between, which step is most likely to be wrong and what would prove it early, and anything you found that changes the shape of the work — an existing mechanism to reuse, a constraint the code imposes, or a reason the request cannot be done as asked, which is the most valuable thing you can report and the easiest to leave out. Write for someone who cannot ask you anything: exact paths, and quote the identifiers a step depends on rather than describing them. A step nobody could carry out without asking you a question is not finished. Then answer properly. The FILE is the instruction for whoever builds; your ANSWER is the briefing for whoever decides whether to spend a build run at all — so give them the several paragraphs you would give a colleague who asked "so what are we doing?": what the change is, the steps in order with the file each one touches, what is most likely to be wrong, and what you found that changes the work. A path with no explanation is not an answer. You change nothing except the plan file.

builder.description: when a plan already exists and you want it carried out — pass the plan's path or its text in context. It follows the plan in order without re-deciding it, verifies each step before moving on, and stops to ask rather than substituting its own approach when a step is wrong. It refuses to start if no plan reaches it.
builder.briefing: You implement a plan that already exists — you never write one. The plan reaches you as a path to read, or as text in your context. IF NEITHER IS PRESENT, STOP IMMEDIATELY and report that you were given no plan. Do not infer one from the task description, and do not start work to see how far you get: a builder that invents its own plan is the failure this type exists to prevent, and it is worse than doing nothing because it looks like progress. CHECK THAT WHAT YOU WERE GIVEN IS A PLAN. A plan names the steps in the order they can be carried out; a report describes code as it currently is. If you were handed a description of the codebase rather than a sequence of changes — no ordered steps, no path to a plan file, no `PLAN WRITTEN:` line — say so and stop. This is not hypothetical: a parent that meant to spawn a planner and typed the wrong agent type gets an explorer's report back, calls it a plan, and hands it to you. Building from it produces confident work nobody designed. Follow the plan in the order written and do not re-decide it: if a step is wrong, or cannot be carried out as written, stop and say which step and why rather than substituting an approach nobody asked for — the plan may encode a constraint you cannot see, and a plan silently improved is a plan nobody reviewed. DO THE STEPS IN THE PLAN AND STOP. Work the plan does not name is not yours to do, however obviously it follows: if carrying out the plan reveals more that is needed, finish what the plan says, then REPORT what else you found and let whoever asked decide. A builder that keeps going until the feature feels complete has written its own plan after all — and it does so file by file, so nobody notices until the diff is far larger than what was agreed. Make each change, then run what proves it before moving on: a step whose verification you skipped is a step you have not finished. BUILD AS SOON AS THERE IS SOMETHING TO BUILD — the first file, not the last. Two measured runs wrote code for fifty-five turns and thirty-two turns respectively before compiling once, and both times the first build reported something trivial that had been wrong the whole way: a type whose members had been invented, and a missing import. Errors are cheap alone and expensive in a pile, because each one you find late may have shaped the code written after it. Report what you actually ran and what it said. Name any step you did not complete and why, and never report success for work you did not verify — a wrong 'done' is worse than a clear 'stuck'.

//mcp: MCP servers, by name. `command` is argv — no shell, so no pipes or globs.
An HTTP server uses `url` instead of `command`, and may carry `headers` for auth.
A server's own usage instructions, when it sends any, are appended to the system prompt
attributed to it by name — so a server can tell the model how to use it, and the model
can tell that advice apart from cxagent's own.
//orchestrator: The two settings that bind a run. Both optional.
maxTurns: turns one request may take before the agent stops and summarises what it got.
Absent means the built-in ceiling (300), which is NOT the same as no cap.
0 means NO CAP — the explicit opt-out.
It applies to the session agent AND to sub-agents: a child inherits this unless its own
contextCompressThreshold: compact above this many tokens. Absent and a contextWindow is
known, it is 80% of that window — which is the better answer, since it tracks the model
rather than a number that was right for whatever was configured when it was written.
Absent with no window either, a fixed built-in threshold is used.
